In [[additive combinatorics]], the '''Plünnecke–Ruzsa inequality''' is an inequality that bounds the size of various [[sumset]]s of a set <math>B</math>, given that there is another set <math>A</math> so that <math>A+B</math> is not much larger than <math>A</math>. A slightly weaker version of this inequality was originally proven and published by Helmut Plünnecke (1970).<ref name=Plu>{{cite journal|last=Plünnecke|first=Helmut|title=Eine zahlentheoretische Anwendung der Graphtheorie|journal=[[Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik]]|volume=243|date=1970|pages=171–183|doi=10.1515/crll.1970.243.171}}</ref>
[[Imre Ruzsa]] (1989)<ref>{{cite journal|last=Ruzsa|first=Imre|title=An application of graph theory to additive number theory|journal=Scientia, Series A|volume=3|date=1989|pages=97–109}}</ref> later published a simpler proof of the current, more general, version of the inequality.
The inequality forms a crucial step in the proof of [[Freiman's theorem]].

==Statement==

The following [[sumset]] notation is standard in additive combinatorics. For subsets <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> of an [[abelian group]] and a natural number <math>k</math>, the following are defined:
* <math>A+B=\{a+b:a\in A,b\in B\}</math>
* <math>A-B=\{a-b:a\in A,b\in B\}</math>
* <math>kA=\underbrace{A+A+\cdots+A}_{k\text{ times}}</math>
The set <math>A + B</math> is known as the '''sumset''' of <math>A</math> and <math>B</math>.

===Plünnecke-Ruzsa inequality===
The most commonly cited version of the statement of the Plünnecke–Ruzsa inequality is the following.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Candela|first1=Pablo|last2=González-Sánchez|first2=Diego|last3=de Roton|first3=Anne|arxiv=1712.07615|title=A Plünnecke-Ruzsa inequality in compact abelian groups|journal=Revista Matemática Iberoamericana|volume=35|issue=7|date=2019|pages=2169–2186|doi=10.4171/rmi/1116}}</ref>

{{math_theorem|note = Plünnecke-Ruzsa inequality|math_statement =If <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> are finite subsets of an abelian group and <math>K</math> is a constant so that <math>|A+B|\le K|A|</math>, then for all nonnegative integers <math>m</math> and <math>n</math>, 
: <math>|mB-nB|\le K^{m+n}|A|.</math>}}

This is often used when <math>A = B</math>, in which case the constant <math>K = |2A|/|A|</math> is known as the '''doubling constant''' of <math>A</math>. In this case, the Plünnecke–Ruzsa inequality states that sumsets formed from a set with small doubling constant must also be small.

===Plünnecke's inequality===
The version of this inequality that was originally proven by Plünnecke (1970)<ref name=Plu /> is slightly weaker.

{{math_theorem|note = Plünnecke's inequality|math_statement = Suppose <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> are finite subsets of an abelian group and <math>K</math> is a constant so that <math>|A+B|\le K|A|</math>. Then for all nonnegative integer <math>m</math>, 
<math>|mB|\le K^m|A|.</math>}}

==Proof==

===Ruzsa triangle inequality===
{{main|Ruzsa triangle inequality}} <!-- The referenced article on the Ruzsa triangle inequality is currently a draft and has been submitted concurrently with this one. -->

The Ruzsa triangle inequality is an important tool which is used to generalize Plünnecke's inequality to the Plünnecke–Ruzsa inequality. Its statement is:

{{math_theorem|note = Ruzsa triangle inequality|math_statement = If <math>A</math>, <math>B</math>, and <math>C</math> are finite subsets of a group, then 
:<math>|A||B-C|\le|A-B||A-C|.</math>}}

<!--
'''Proof'''. To demonstrate this, it suffices to construct an injection from the set <math>A\times(B-C)</math> to the set <math>(A-B)\times(A-C)</math>. Define a function, <math>\phi</math> as follows. For each <math>x\in B-C</math> choose a <math>b(x)\in B</math> and a <math>c(x)\in C</math> such that <math>x=b(x)-c(x)</math>. By the definition of <math>B-C</math>, this can always be done. Let <math>\phi:A\times(B-C)\rightarrow(A-B)\times(A-C)</math> be the function that sends <math>(a,x)</math> to <math>(a-b(x),a-c(x))</math>. For every point <math>\phi(a,x)=(y,z)</math> in the set is <math>(A-B)\times(A-C)</math>, it must be the case that <math>x=z-y</math> and <math>a=y+b(x)</math>. Hence, <math>\phi</math> maps every point in <math>A\times(B-C)</math> to a distinct point in <math>(A-B)\times(A-C)</math> and is thus an injection. In particular, there must be at least as many points in <math>(A-B)\times(A-C)</math> as in <math>A\times(B-C)</math>. Therefore,
:<math>|A||B-C|=|A\times(B-C)|\le|(A-B)\times(A-C)=|A-B||A-C|,</math>
completing the proof. -->

===Proof of Plünnecke-Ruzsa inequality===

The following simple proof of the Plünnecke–Ruzsa inequality is due to Petridis (2014).<ref>{{cite book|last=Petridis|first=Giorgis|title=Combinatorial and Additive Number Theory|chapter=The Plünnecke–Ruzsa Inequality: An Overview|volume=101|date=2014|pages=229–241|doi=10.1007/978-1-4939-1601-6_16|doi-access=free|series=Springer Proceedings in Mathematics & Statistics|isbn=978-1-4939-1600-9}}</ref>
<!-- The following proof is due to Petridis [reference paper] and demonstrates the following slightly stronger statement: {{math_theorem|note=Plünnecke-Ruzsa inequality|math_statement = If <math>A,B</math> are finite subsets of an abelian group such that <math>|A+B|\le K|A|</math>, then for all nonnegative integers <math>m,n,</math> 
:<math>|mB-nB|\le K^{m+n}|A|.</math>}} -->

'''Lemma:''' Let <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> be finite subsets of an abelian group <math>G</math>. If <math>X\subseteq A</math> is a nonempty subset that minimizes the value of <math>K'=|X+B|/|X|</math>, then for all finite subsets <math>C\subset G</math>, 
:<math>|X+B+C|\le K'|X+C|.</math>

'''Proof:''' This is demonstrated by induction on the size of <math>|C|</math>. For the base case of <math>|C|=1</math>, note that <math>S+C</math> is simply a translation of <math>S</math> for any <math>S\subseteq G</math>, so 
:<math>|X+B+C|=|X+B|=K'|X|=K'|X+C|.</math>
For the inductive step, assume the inequality holds for all <math>C\subseteq G</math> with <math>|C|\le n</math> for some positive integer <math>n</math>. Let <math>C</math> be a subset of <math>G</math> with <math>|C|=n+1</math>, and let <math>C=C'\sqcup\{\gamma\}</math> for some <math>\gamma\in C</math>. (In particular, the inequality holds for <math>C'</math>.) Finally, let <math>Z=\{x\in X: x+B+\{\gamma\}\subseteq X+B+C'\}</math>. The definition of <math>Z</math> implies that <math>Z+B+\{\gamma\}\subseteq X+B+C'</math>. Thus, by the definition of these sets, 
:<math>X+B+C=(X+B+C')\cup((X+B+\{\gamma\})\backslash(Z+B+\{\gamma\})).</math>
Hence, considering the sizes of the sets, 
:<math>\begin{align}|X+B+C|&\le|X+B+C'|+|(X+B+\{\gamma\})\backslash(Z+B+\{\gamma\})|\\&=|X+B+C'|+|X+B+\{\gamma\}|-|Z+B+\{\gamma\}|\\&=|X+B+C'|+|X+B|-|Z+B|.\end{align}</math>
The definition of <math>Z</math> implies that <math>Z\subseteq X\subseteq A</math>, so by the definition of <math>X</math>, <math>|Z+B|\ge K'|Z|</math>. Thus, applying the inductive hypothesis on <math>C'</math> and using the definition of <math>X</math>, 
:<math>\begin{align}|X+B+C|&\le|X+B+C'|+|X+B|-|Z+B|\\&\le K'|X+C'|+|X+B|-|Z+B|\\&\le K'|X+C'|+K'|X|-|Z+B|\\&\le K'|X+C'|+K'|X|-K'|Z|\\&=K'(|X+C'|+|X|-|Z|).\end{align}</math>
To bound the right side of this inequality, let <math>W=\{x\in X:x+\gamma\in X+C'\}</math>. Suppose <math>y\in X+C'</math> and <math>y\in X+\{\gamma\}</math>, then there exists <math>x\in X</math> such that <math>x+\gamma=y\in X+C'</math>. Thus, by definition, <math>x\in W</math>, so <math>y\in W+\{\gamma\}</math>. Hence, the sets <math>X+C'</math> and <math>(X+\{\gamma\})\backslash(W+\{\gamma\})</math> are disjoint. The definitions of <math>W</math> and <math>C'</math> thus imply that 
:<math>X+C=(X+C')\sqcup((X+\{\gamma\})\backslash(W+\{\gamma\})).</math>
Again by definition, <math>W\subseteq Z</math>, so <math>|W|\le|Z|</math>. Hence, 
:<math>\begin{align}|X+C|&=|X+C'|+|(X+\{\gamma\})\backslash(W+\{\gamma\})|\\&=|X+C'|+|X+\{\gamma\}|-|W+\{\gamma\}|\\&=|X+C'|+|X|-|W|\\&\ge|X+C'|+|X|-|Z|.\end{align}</math>
Putting the above two inequalities together gives 
:<math>|X+B+C|\le K'(|X+C'|+|X|-|Z|)\le K'|X+C|.</math>
This completes the proof of the lemma.

To prove the Plünnecke–Ruzsa inequality, take <math>X</math> and <math>K'</math> as in the statement of the lemma. It is first necessary to show that 
:<math>|X+nB|\le K^n|X|.</math>
This can be proved by induction. For the base case, the definitions of <math>K</math> and <math>K'</math> imply that <math>K'\le K</math>. Thus, the definition of <math>X</math> implies that <math>|X+B|\le K|X|</math>. For inductive step, suppose this is true for <math>n=j</math>. Applying the lemma with <math>C=jB</math> and the inductive hypothesis gives 
:<math>|X+(j+1)B|\le K'|X+jB|\le K|X+jB|\le K^{j+1}|X|.</math>
This completes the induction. Finally, the Ruzsa triangle inequality gives 
:<math>|mB-nB|\le\frac{|X+mB||X+nB|}{|X|}\le\frac{K^m|X|K^n|X|}{|X|}=K^{m+n}|X|.</math>
Because <math>X\subseteq A</math>, it must be the case that <math>|X|\le |A|</math>. Therefore, 
:<math>|mB-nB|\le K^{m+n}|A|.</math>
This completes the proof of the Plünnecke–Ruzsa inequality.

==Plünnecke graphs==

Both Plünnecke's proof of Plünnecke's inequality and Ruzsa's original proof of the Plünnecke–Ruzsa inequality use the method of Plünnecke graphs. Plünnecke graphs are a way to capture the additive structure of the sets <math>A, A+B, A+2B, \dots</math> in a graph theoretic manner<ref name=TaoVu>{{cite book|last1=Tao|first1=T.|last2=Vu|first2=V.|date=2006|title=Additive Combinatorics|location=Cambridge|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-85386-6}}</ref><ref>{{Citation|last=Ruzsa|first=I.|title=Sumsets and structure|url=https://www.math.cmu.edu/users/af1p/Teaching/AdditiveCombinatorics/Additive-Combinatorics.pdf}}.</ref>

To define a Plünnecke graph we first define commutative graphs and layered graphs:

'''Definition'''. A [[directed graph]] <math>G</math> is called '''semicommutative''' if, whenever there exist distinct <math>x, y, z_1, z_2, \dots, z_k</math> such that <math>(x, y)</math> and <math>(y, z_i)</math> are edges in <math>G</math> for each <math>i</math>, then there also exist distinct <math>y_1, y_2, \dots, y_k</math> so that <math>(x, y_i)</math> and <math>(y_i, z_i)</math> are edges in <math>G</math> for each <math>i</math>.

<math>G</math> is called '''commutative''' if it is semicommutative and the graph formed by reversing all its edges is also semicommutative.

'''Definition'''. A '''layered graph''' is a (directed) graph <math>G</math> whose vertex set can be partitioned <math>V_0 \cup V_1 \cup \dots \cup V_m</math> so that all edges in <math>G</math> are from <math>V_i</math> to <math>V_{i+1}</math>, for some <math>i</math>.

'''Definition'''.  A '''Plünnecke graph''' is a layered graph which is commutative.

The canonical example of a Plünnecke graph is the following, which shows how the structure of the sets <math>A, A+B, A+2B, \dots, A + mB</math> form a Plünnecke graph.

'''Example'''. Let <math>A, B</math> be subsets of an abelian group. Then, let <math>G</math> be the layered graph so that each layer <math>V_j</math> is a copy of <math>A + jB</math>, so that <math>V_0 = A</math>, <math>V_1 = A + B</math>, ...,  <math>V_m = A + mB</math>. Create the edge <math>(x, y)</math> (where <math>x \in V_i</math> and <math>y \in V_{i+1}</math>) whenever there exists <math>b \in B</math> such that <math>y = x + b</math>. (In particular, if <math>x \in V_i</math>, then <math>x + b \in V_{i+1}</math> by definition, so every vertex has [[Directed graph#Indegree and outdegree|outdegree]] equal to the size of <math>B</math>.) 
Then <math>G</math> is a Plünnecke graph. For example, to check that <math>G</math> is semicommutative, if <math>(x, y)</math> and <math>(y, z_i)</math> are edges in <math>G</math> for each <math>i</math>, then <math>y - x, z_i - y \in B</math>. Then, let <math>y_i = x + z_i - y</math>, so that <math>y_i - x = z_i - y \in B</math> and <math>z_i - y_i = y - x \in B</math>. Thus, <math>G</math> is semicommutative. It can be similarly checked that the graph formed by reversing all edges of <math>G</math> is also semicommutative, so <math>G</math> is a Plünnecke graph.

In a Plünnecke graph, the '''image''' of a set <math>X \subseteq V_0</math> in <math>V_j</math>, written <math>\text{im}(X, V_j)</math>, is defined to be the set of vertices in <math>V_j</math> which can be reached by a path starting from some vertex in <math>X</math>. In particular, in the aforementioned example, <math>\text{im}(X, V_j)</math> is just <math>X + jB</math>.

The '''magnification ratio''' between <math>V_0</math> and <math>V_j</math>, denoted <math>\mu_j(G)</math>, is then defined as the minimum factor by which the image of a set must exceed the size of the original set. Formally, 
:<math>\mu_j(G) = \min_{X \subseteq V_0, X \neq \emptyset} \frac{|\text{im}(X, V_j)|}{|X|}.</math>

Plünnecke's theorem is the following statement about Plünnecke graphs.

{{math theorem|note=Plünnecke's theorem|math_statement=Let <math>G</math> be a Plünnecke graph. Then, <math>\mu_j(G)^{1/j}</math> is decreasing in <math>j</math>.}}

The proof of Plünnecke's theorem involves a technique known as the "tensor product trick", in addition to an application of [[Menger's theorem]].<ref name=TaoVu/>

The Plünnecke–Ruzsa inequality is a fairly direct consequence of Plünnecke's theorem and the Ruzsa triangle inequality. Applying Plünnecke's theorem to the graph given in the example, at <math>j = m</math> and <math>j = 1</math>, yields that if <math>|A + B| / |A| = K</math>, then there exists <math>X \subseteq A</math> so that <math>|X + mB| / |X| \le K^m</math>. Applying this result once again with <math>X</math> instead of <math>A</math>, there exists <math>X' \subseteq X</math> so that <math>|X' + nB| / |X'| \le K^n</math>. Then, by Ruzsa's triangle inequality (on <math>-X', mB, nB</math>), 
:<math>|mB - nB| \le |X' + mB||X' + nB|/|X'| \le K^{m}|X| K^{n} = K^{m+n}|X|,</math>
thus proving the Plünnecke–Ruzsa inequality.

<!--
==Variants of Ruzsa's triangle inequality==

A corollary of the Plünnecke-Ruzsa inequality is Ruzsa's sum triangle inequality. {{math_theorem|note = Ruzsa's sum triangle inequality|math_statement = If <math>A</math>, <math>B</math>, and <math>C</math> are finite subsets of an abelian group, then
:<math>|A||B+C|\le|A+B||A+C|.</math>}}

'''Proof:''' If <math>A</math> is the empty set, then the left side of the inequality becomes <math>0</math>, so the inequality is true. Otherwise, let <math>X</math> be a subset of <math>A</math> that minimizes <math>K'=|X+B|/|X|</math>. Let <math>K=|A+B|/|A|</math>. The definition of <math>X</math> implies that <math>K'\le K</math>. Because <math>X\subseteq A</math>, applying the lemma from the proof of the Plünnecke-Ruzsa inequality gives 
:<math>|B+C|\le|X+B+C|\le K'|X+C|\le K'|A+C|\le K|A+C|=\frac{|A+B||A+C|}{|A|}.</math> 
Rearranging gives Ruzsa's sum triangle inequality.

By replacing <math>B</math> and <math>C</math> in Ruzsa's triangle inequality and Ruzsa's sum triangle inequality with <math>-B</math> and <math>-C</math> as needed, a more general result can be obtained: If <math>A</math>, <math>B</math>, and <math>C</math> are finite subsets of an abelian group then 
:<math>|A||B\pm C|\le|A\pm B||A\pm C|,</math>
where all eight possible configurations of signs hold. These results are also sometimes known collectively as '''Ruzsa's triangle inequalities'''.
